title: The mobile visit for a creative studio

excerpt: The first phone screen still has to show one decision and a way to start a project. Do not let the desktop layout decide the phone page.

faqs.question: What has to be on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The decision, the work that proves it, and a way to start a project, with enough quiet to read them. A reel, a newsletter, and a cookie wall should not push that trio below the fold.

faqs.question: How do you test the mobile page?
faqs.answer: Open it on a phone you did not design on, in a hallway, and say the decision and the next step after ten seconds. Then tap the action and confirm the next page explains what happens. If you only check the desktop file, you have not reviewed the visit you will get.

faqs.question: What should you cut when the screen gets narrow?
faqs.answer: The logo wall, the wide reel, decorative marquees, and any image that existed to balance a desktop composition. Rewrite comparisons as stacked, labeled pictures. Do not only shrink the desktop.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
Most clients who have already seen fifty portfolios will judge the creative studio mobile website before they ever open it on a desk. The first screen still has to show one decision in the work and a way to start a project. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page.

A wide layout that collapses into a stack of cropped type, a tiny reel, and a button below the fold is not a mobile visit. It is a desktop page that survived export. This buyer will not rotate their phone to give you the benefit of the doubt.

## The phone is the review

Assume the link arrives in a message. They open it in the street, in a meeting, between two other studios. The tab is one of many. You do not get a calm desk and a large monitor unless you have already earned a second look. Design the first look for the glass in their hand.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the time budget. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear in about 10. They read only about a quarter of the text. On a phone the quarter is even more literal, because the screen holds less. The value, for this buyer, is one decision they can see, plus a way to start. If that pair is not in the first viewport, the rest of your craft is a rumor.

Do the review yourself on a phone you did not design on. Load the page over a normal connection. Do not cradle the device in a flattering light and call it QA. Ask a person who has not seen the desktop to say what the studio does and how they would hire it. If they mention the animation and not the decision, the phone page is still a reel.

Treat the phone as the original, and the wide screen as a place you may add, carefully. Teams that design the desktop first tend to protect the desktop. They scale type down, they stack columns in a random order, and they keep a horizontal film that letterboxes into a stripe. The phone then looks like an apology. Start from the sentence and the frame that fit a narrow column. Add the side-by-side only when there is width to earn it.

## The first screen

The first screen needs four things, and no fifth thing that pushes them down. The sentence of the decision. The work that proves it. The action, Start a project. Enough quiet that those three can be read. A logo can sit in the bar. A tagline that repeats the sentence cannot. A cookie wall that eats the screen cannot, if you can avoid it. A newsletter field cannot.

The sentence should wrap in two or three lines, not six. If your headline only works as one long line on a 1440-pixel canvas, it is not a headline for this buyer. Rewrite it until it is true at a narrow measure. Short sentences are not a style preference here. They are how the first screen stays the first screen.

The image should be the decision, cropped for the width. A layout that depended on three columns must be re-cropped, not squeezed. If the decision was a comparison, stack the before and the after with labels, or show the after and put the before one tap away. Do not ship a crop that cuts off the part of the interface you were proud of. That is how a good project becomes a mysterious texture.

The action should be visible without a hunt. Same words as the desktop. Large enough to tap. Not glued to the very bottom in a bar that covers the work, and not floating over the sentence. Give it a place in the flow, then repeat it after the first proof. One path, twice, is clarity. A sticky bar plus a chat bubble plus a text link is three paths.

## Do not shrink the desktop

Shrinking is the failure mode. Type that was elegant at 72 pixels on a monitor becomes a poster on a phone, and the next paragraph starts halfway down the city. Or the opposite: everything scales so faithfully that body text is too small to read, and the buyer pinches. Pinch-to-read is a bug.

Set type for the phone in actual sizes you have read on a device. A line length of reasonable words. Space between blocks so the sentence, the image, and the action are separate ideas. Alignment that does not depend on a mouse hovering. Hover is not a mobile event. If a caption only appears on hover, the phone visitor never gets the decision.

Navigation has to open into the same jobs as the wide bar. Work, services, about, start a project. Do not hide Start a project inside a footer that takes four swipes. Do not replace the menu with a gesture nobody will guess. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the plain requirement: the interface has to be operable, and the text has to be perceivable. A hairline menu on a bright phone fails people with ordinary eyes, which means it fails your buyer.

Motion should be quieter on the phone, not louder. A parallax hero that hitches is not craft. It is a reason to leave. If you use motion, keep it short, keep it tied to a change of state, and respect reduced motion. A studio that sells care and then traps someone in an unstoppable film has already contradicted the pitch.

## What survives a narrow column

Make a keep list and a cut list before you adjust breakpoints.

Keep the decision sentence, the proof image, the action, and the name of the studio. Keep one secondary proof if it shows a different kind of choice. Keep a way back to work, services, and about.

Cut the reel that needed a wide frame. Cut the logo wall. Cut the three-column process. Cut decorative numbers and marquee text that crawls sideways. Cut any image whose only job was to balance a desktop composition. On a phone, balance is vertical. Extra ornaments become obstacles between the buyer and the action.

Rewrite, do not just reflow. A paragraph that was a caption beside an image may need to move above the image so they know what they are about to see. A comparison that was a slider may need to become two labeled pictures. A table of prices may need to become stacked offers. If the only instruction to engineering is "make it responsive," you have postponed the design.

Test real content. A name that wraps badly. A project title that is two lines longer than the sample. A button label that no longer fits. The phone page is where optimistic sample content goes to fail. Use the real decision and the real project names.

Forms, if any appear this early, should be shorter than you think. Email and a sentence, or no form at all and a link to the contact path. Ten fields on a phone is how you lose the project you just earned. The contact page can ask for more, and even there it should ask for little.

## Speed is part of the first screen

A decision they cannot see yet is not a decision. Heavy images, an unoptimized film, and a page that jumps while loading will spend the ten seconds on a spinner. Google's Core Web Vitals are the practical bar: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. Those thresholds live in [Google's Core Web Vitals documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals). They are targets for the page the buyer actually loads, which is often the phone.

Serve an image that fits the phone, not the desktop file scaled down by the browser after a long download. Give the hero a known size so the layout does not jump when it arrives. Do not autoplay a reel in the hero. If you need motion, ship it after the sentence is readable, or do not ship it.

A static page with a sharp picture will feel faster than a clever page that loads a studio's worth of scripts. Hanabi builds marketing sites to be fast before they are clever, in Next.js on Vercel, with images that have a size and a job. You do not have to copy the stack. You do have to refuse a hero that costs the first ten seconds.

Test on a middling phone, not only on the newest one in the studio. If the page is smooth only on your device, it is not smooth.

## A review you can do in a hallway

Walk outside or into a hallway and open the homepage. Start a timer. After ten seconds, look up and say the decision and the next step. If you cannot, the first screen is wrong. Do not go back to the desktop file to admire it. Change the phone screen.

Then open one proof page. The constraint and the decision should be readable before a gallery. Then tap the action. The next page should load quickly and tell you what happens after you reach out. If any of those three fails, you do not have a mobile visit. You have a set of desktop artboards and a hope.

Do this again after launch, on the live URL, because staging data and production images are not the same weight. Ask one person who fits the buyer, a client who has seen many portfolios, to do the same hallway test. Believe them if they cannot find the decision.

The path after that tap is its own page. [A contact path for a creative studio](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-creative-studio) should say what happens next, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is still to start a project. A form with ten fields will waste the visit you just designed the phone to win.

When you want a site reviewed at that width, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) on your phone first. See whether a decision survives the column. Then hold your own first screen to the same test before you add another section.
